A1.justification: Both PDFs describe UrbanVerse, with matching authors, core pipeline, datasets, and experiments. Text extraction and visual inspection cover all 37 pages of v1 and 43 pages of v2, including their appendices, supporting reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original scene-reconstruction experiments, a 32-participant human evaluation, navigation scaling experiments, real-world robot trials, and target-specific fine-tuning results.

after.justification: v2 retains those original results and adds quantitative physical-attribute validation, a training-scene horizon experiment, and computational measurements.

M1.justification: Section 3.2 adds an explicit ORCA-based dynamic-agent population component, using occupancy maps, sampled start-goal pairs, and online velocity adjustment. The core scene-distillation, asset-retrieval, scene-assembly, and PPO procedures remain unchanged; the PDFs do not establish that the retained navigation experiments used this additional component.

E1.justification: Appendix C.4 adds quantitative evaluation of physical-attribute annotations against reference dimensions and masses for 17 object categories. The original KITTI-360, UrbanVerse, AutoBench, CraftBench, and real-world navigation coverage is retained. Illustrations of additional supported tasks do not establish additional policy benchmarks.

E2.justification: Comparator membership is unchanged in the matched reconstruction, CraftBench, real-world navigation, and target-specific fine-tuning experiments. The new efficiency comparison reuses UrbanSim, which was already evaluated against UrbanVerse; the new simulator feature table does not establish additional experimentally evaluated baselines.

E3.justification: The added horizon experiment compares 320 approximately 100 m scene segments with the original 160 approximately 200 m scenes, evaluating on CraftBench. New protocols also specify physical-attribute evaluation on 1,335 objects using MAPE and timing measurements across video lengths and GPU configurations. Existing navigation budgets, architecture, and testing settings are retained.

E4.justification: v2 substantially expands system validation through physical-annotation accuracy checks, a half-length versus full-length training-scene ablation, illustrated reconstruction failures, and computational scaling analysis in Appendices C.4, F, H, and K. These test previously unexamined aspects of annotation reliability, training-horizon benefits, failure mechanisms, and practical scalability.

E5.justification: New Table 6 explicitly reports standard deviations alongside physical-attribute percentage errors. This adds dispersion reporting across evaluated objects, without establishing additional stochastic runs. The five-run simulated evaluation and three-repeat real-world evaluation statements remain unchanged.

E6.justification: New results include average height, length, width, and mass errors of 5.88%, 6.14%, 7.00%, and 19.58%; half-length training SR of 32.3 versus the retained full-length result of 41.9; and generation, annotation, and rendering measurements. Existing reconstruction, human-study, navigation, and per-scene robot results are unchanged. Reported asset totals change from 102,530 to 102,444 and leaf categories from 667 to 659.

T1.justification: The scene-graph formulation, power-law relationship, and PPO reward equation are retained. The added standard MAPE formula and navigation-metric explanations document evaluation measures without introducing new theoretical reasoning, assumptions, propositions, or proofs.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and central conclusion retain the same contributions and headline claims: video-grounded simulation, the annotated asset repository, policy scaling, and zero-shot transfer. The reported +6.3 simulation and +30.1 real-world success improvements are unchanged; added supporting analyses do not redefine these claims.

C2.justification: v2 adds explicit applicability limits and explanations of failures involving difficult terrain, lighting, occlusion, and depth or pose drift. It also interprets appearance mismatches as potentially benign randomization, mass errors as material uncertainty, and longer training scenes as providing richer decision-making experience. The original interpretation of navigation generalization remains intact.

D1.justification: New documentation covers the user workflow, supported inputs and observation modalities, every-tenth-frame quality screening, generation hardware, LLM call counts, and runtime and annotation costs. Appendix L.1 also spells out navigation metrics. Existing implementation backbones, PPO hyperparameters, robot configurations, and future-tense resource-release commitments are retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds the ORCA reference by Van Den Berg et al. and replaces the Dorbala et al. citation with Mittal et al.'s Isaac Lab reference in simulation implementation discussions. Related work more explicitly distinguishes editable digital cousins from fused 3DGS digital twins, while preserving the overall research positioning.

P1.justification: Most main-text prose and its organization remain intact. Local revisions include the related-work explanation, a shortened demonstration-page description, an expanded appendix guide, a user-workflow section, an LLM-use declaration, and conference-header and acknowledgment updates. The added scientific sections do not amount to a wholesale narrative rewrite.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the visual presentation with dynamic-agent and task illustrations, a user-workflow diagram, challenging-input and failure examples, and tables for physical validation, horizon ablation, and computational costs. It also adds a main-text simulator comparison and reorganizes existing displays, including moving asset-recovery scores to the final column of the reconstruction table.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1's qualitative physical-scale validation and attribution of robustness to long training scenes, v2 supplies quantitative attribute errors and a direct horizon comparison, alongside useful failure and cost reporting. These strengthen support and transparency, although validation covers a limited asset subset. The new time-based collision metric definition is also difficult to reconcile with retained collision-triggered episode termination, leaving an evaluation ambiguity.
